chunks.title: ME-3310 Fluids: continuity, pipe flow, and head loss
chunks.text: For steady incompressible flow through a pipe, conservation of mass reduces to constant volume flow rate. The useful relation is Q = A V, where A is the cross-sectional area and V is the section-average velocity. A circular pipe has area pi D squared divided by four. Therefore doubling the diameter at constant volume flow rate divides velocity by four. Always decide which variable is fixed before making a scaling argument. Holding velocity fixed instead would increase the volume flow rate by four. Density cancels only when the fluid is effectively incompressible and has the same density at both sections. The Darcy-Weisbach equation gives frictional head loss as hL = f (L/D) V squared divided by 2g. The Darcy friction factor differs from the Fanning factor by a factor of four. In laminar circular-pipe flow the Darcy factor is 64/Re, with Reynolds number Re = rho V D / mu. In the fully rough turbulent limit, the friction factor depends on relative roughness and becomes effectively independent of Reynolds number. At fixed geometry in that limit, doubling velocity quadruples the head loss. This does not hold if the flow crosses regimes or relative roughness changes. For fully developed laminar flow at fixed Q and fixed pipe length, substituting continuity and the laminar friction factor shows pressure drop is proportional to Q divided by D to the fourth power. Doubling diameter reduces pressure drop by sixteen. Bernoulli's ideal relation excludes losses and shaft work; its extended energy equation includes both. Pressure and head have different units. Multiply a head in metres by rho g to obtain a pressure in pascals. Pump power delivered to the fluid equals rho g Q hp; required shaft power is larger when efficiency is below unity.

chunks.title: ENGR-2300 Thermodynamics: first law and heat-engine limits
chunks.text: Adopt the convention that heat entering a closed system is positive and work done by the system is positive. The first law then reads delta U = Q - W when kinetic and potential energy changes are negligible. A rigid tank has no moving-boundary work because its volume is constant. An insulated tank has no heat transfer, but its internal energy may still change if a paddle wheel supplies shaft work. Adiabatic does not mean isothermal. An ideal gas undergoing a temperature change has internal-energy change m cv delta T when a constant specific heat approximation is reasonable. A steady-flow control volume uses enthalpy because fluid crosses its boundaries while doing flow work. For a steady adiabatic turbine with negligible velocity and elevation changes, specific shaft work leaving the control volume equals hin minus hout. For a throttling valve with no shaft work and negligible kinetic and potential changes, hin approximately equals hout. Throttling is not generally isentropic. Pressure falls through an irreversible restriction, and entropy usually increases. An ideal gas with enthalpy depending only on temperature has no temperature change during ideal throttling, while real fluids may cool or warm. A heat engine receives heat QH from a hot reservoir and rejects QC to a cold reservoir. Its thermal efficiency is Wnet divided by QH, or one minus QC divided by QH. The reversible upper bound between two reservoirs is one minus TC divided by TH. Temperatures in this expression must be absolute kelvin. A device operating between 600 K and 300 K cannot exceed fifty percent efficiency. Actual engines perform worse because of irreversibilities and practical constraints. The Carnot bound compares devices between the same reservoirs; it does not predict an actual engine's power output. Use energy balances before selecting property relations and check every sign against the stated control boundary.

chunks.title: ME-2010 Statics: equilibrium, moments, and supports
chunks.text: A planar rigid body in static equilibrium satisfies three independent scalar equations: the sums of horizontal forces, vertical forces, and moments are each zero. Draw a free-body diagram before writing equations. Isolate one body and replace each support by its reaction components. An ideal planar pin supplies two force components and no reaction couple. A frictionless roller supplies one force normal to its contact surface. A fixed support supplies two forces and a moment. Counting unknowns helps identify whether a problem can be solved by rigid-body equilibrium alone. The moment of a force about a point is the cross product of position and force. In a plane its signed magnitude is F times the perpendicular distance from the reference point to the force's line of action. A force acting through the reference point contributes zero moment, even if its point of application is far away. Choose a moment center that eliminates unknown reactions when possible. State a consistent positive rotation convention; counterclockwise is common. A pure couple has the same moment about every reference point and cannot be replaced by a lone force. For a simply supported beam with a point load P centered on a span L, symmetry and equilibrium give support reactions P/2. A uniform distributed load w over the full span is equivalent, for overall equilibrium, to a force wL at the span midpoint. The equivalent force preserves resultant force and moment, but does not preserve the internal shear and bending moment distribution at every section. For a triangular distributed load, the resultant is half the base times the peak intensity and acts one third of the base from the larger-intensity end. Check dimensions: distributed load is force per length; its resultant is force. A solved equilibrium equation cannot correct a missing or incorrectly directed force on the original diagram.

chunks.title: ME-3310 Fluids: pipe networks and minor losses
chunks.text: When pipes connect in series, the same steady volume flow passes through every segment, while the total head loss is the sum of the losses in each segment and fitting. A useful bookkeeping form is hL = [f(L/D) + sum(K)] V squared divided by 2g, with each velocity evaluated in the pipe or fitting reference area used to define its coefficient. The Darcy friction factor f is dimensionless, as are the minor-loss coefficients K. A sudden expansion can also be modeled with a loss coefficient, but its value depends on the area ratio and the chosen upstream velocity. Do not add a fitting loss using a velocity from a different diameter without converting the coefficient consistently. For parallel branches joining the same two junctions, the head drop across each branch is equal, while the branch flow rates add to the total. Equal head loss does not generally mean equal flow: branch length, diameter, roughness, fluid properties, and fittings all matter. A network solution must satisfy both continuity at each junction and an energy equation around each independent loop. In a simple pair of branches with known properties, one can guess a flow split, compute each branch's losses, and adjust the split until the losses agree. The flow that goes to zero in a branch must also produce zero branch loss in the physical limiting case. At a pump, the head rise supplied to the fluid offsets elevation change, pressure change, and irreversible losses around the system. A system curve often rises approximately with flow squared when turbulent friction dominates and reservoir levels stay fixed. The pump operating point is where the pump curve and system curve intersect; it is not chosen by maximizing flow in isolation. Read pump head, efficiency, and power at the same operating flow. If a valve is throttled, added resistance moves the intersection toward lower flow. Conservation of mass still holds, even though the distribution of pressure and head changes throughout the network.

chunks.title: ENGR-2300 Thermodynamics: entropy and refrigeration cycles
chunks.text: The entropy balance helps distinguish energy conservation from the direction of a real process. For a closed system, the entropy change equals entropy transferred with heat plus entropy generated internally. Heat transfer across a boundary at temperature T carries an entropy amount Q/T when T is uniform at the boundary; work carries energy but no entropy. Entropy generation is nonnegative for a real process and is zero only for an internally reversible idealization. An insulated process has no entropy transfer by heat, but it can still generate entropy through friction, mixing, or an unrestrained expansion. Thus adiabatic does not imply isentropic. For a control volume at steady state, mass and energy flow through the boundary, and entropy can be transported with those streams. A turbine may produce less work than its isentropic reference because irreversibility raises the outlet entropy. Isentropic efficiency compares actual performance with that ideal reference at the same inlet state and outlet pressure. It is not a general efficiency definition for every device: compressors and pumps use an input-work comparison, while turbines use an output-work comparison. Keep the comparison direction clear before substituting property values. A refrigerator removes heat QL from a cold space and requires work input Win, giving coefficient of performance COPR = QL/Win. A heat pump delivers QH to a warm space and has COPHP = QH/Win. For the same cycle, energy conservation gives QH = QL + Win, so COPHP = COPR + 1. These coefficients can exceed one because they measure heat moved per unit work rather than a fraction of energy converted. The reversible Carnot refrigerator between absolute temperatures TL and TH has COPR = TL/(TH - TL); reducing the temperature lift raises the ideal COP. Real equipment performs below this limit because heat transfer and compression are irreversible.

chunks.title: ME-2010 Statics: trusses and internal force cuts
chunks.text: A pin-jointed planar truss is commonly idealized as straight, slender members connected by frictionless pins, with external loads applied only at joints. Under those assumptions each member is a two-force member: its end forces are equal, opposite, and collinear with the member axis. The method of joints isolates one pin at a time and applies the two planar force equilibrium equations. Start at a joint with no more than two unknown member forces, unless another known relation is available. Label a guessed member force as tension, pulling away from the joint; a negative answer then indicates compression under that sign convention. The method of sections cuts through a truss to find selected member forces without solving every joint. Draw a free-body diagram of one side of the cut, include its external loads and support reactions, and use moment equilibrium about a point that eliminates two cut forces when possible. In a planar truss the cut should usually cross no more than three unknown members because only three independent rigid-body equilibrium equations are available. A zero-force member can sometimes be identified before calculation: at an unloaded joint with two non-collinear members, both forces are zero; with three members where two are collinear, the third is zero. These rules rely on the ideal joint and loading assumptions. For beams, internal normal force N, shear V, and bending moment M are exposed by cutting through a section and balancing one side. With a sign convention fixed, a distributed load changes shear along the beam, and shear change corresponds to the area under the load diagram with the appropriate sign. The change in bending moment corresponds to the area under the shear diagram. A concentrated force causes a jump in shear, while a concentrated couple causes a jump in moment. These relationships provide checks on diagrams and boundary values, but the signs depend on the chosen face convention. Always state the convention beside the cut equations and verify units: N and V are forces, while M has force-times-length units.
